svg.title: Encapsulation overhead for the common tunnelling methods, and the three ways to handle the resulting MTU debt
svg.desc: A bar chart of overhead in bytes: MPLS adds 4 to 8 bytes, GRE adds 24, VXLAN adds 50, and VXLAN with IPsec adds roughly 100 to 120. A second scale shows what that means for a 1500 byte payload: the usable MTU falls to about 1450 for VXLAN and about 1400 for VXLAN over IPsec. Three handling options are listed. Raise the MTU on the underlay, which is the only option that does not degrade anything but requires every device on the path. Clamp the TCP MSS at the edge, which fixes TCP but hides the problem from every UDP application. Rely on path MTU discovery, which usually fails because ICMP is filtered. A closing note says to size for the worst encapsulation in the design and to test with a protocol that cannot fragment, because file copy will pass either way.
svg.text: Every encapsulation is paid for out of the same 1500 bytes
The debt is fixed and known in advance; only the decision about who pays it is optional
4–8 B (one or two labels) · usable MTU ~1492
The bars are drawn to scale. Anything that adds more than one header moves the problem into the application's lap.
Set 1600 or 9000 end to end so the
Rewrite the MSS at the edge so TCP
never offers a segment that will not fit.
Fixes TCP only; UDP and ICMP still break.
In most security postures it does not.
Test with something that cannot fragment: a file copy will pass on any MTU because TCP adjusts. Use a large UDP probe or a DNS response over 1400 bytes,
